story_text.value:
35 years ago today (Oct 5, 1991), Linux 0.02 was released.

I made an animated history of Linux using Claude Code + opus 5.5.

I've been experimenting with a “video as code” workflow - source, prompts, assets, and rendering scripts live in Git, and the final video is a generated artifact.

you can try it out here:

Repo: https://github.com/sujee/visual-stories/tree/main/projects/l... | https://github.com/sujee/visual-stories

Video: https://youtu.be/lkOxEeqwMBo

I'm curious what people think of this approach. Is “video as code” useful beyond experiments like this? Love to hear some feedback and experiences.

thank you!

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

In my day to day, I switch between my Windows PC and Macbook often. One thing I find annoying is having to change what keyboard shortcuts I use depending on the OS (e.g. cmd+c vs ctrl+c for copying). It confuses my muscle memory and slows me down.

I first tried using AutoHotkey to bind MacOS-like shortcuts to Windows shortcuts. This worked, but it was hard to configure. I would also have to quit AutoHotkey to get past Anti-Cheat software on some games.

So I decided to create this app in case others also face the same issues as me.

Disclaimer: I built this app using Claude Code. I don't have much experience building windows apps so it would've been difficult to make this on my own.

story_text.value:
I have been working on Rashomon, an open-source execution recorder for AI coding agents.

The basic idea is that the agent transcript is not ground truth. Rashomon keeps its own record of what happened and compares it against the agent’s account.

For Claude Code, it records things like:

* shell commands, exit codes, and whether they may have written files * tool calls and outcomes * test commands and their outcomes * subagent lifecycle and ordering * timestamps and parent/child relationships * keyed digests of command/tool inputs and working directories

It builds a timeline from these events. It does not store prompts, responses, file contents, or tool output.

For example, it now detects patterns like:

`test fails → only test files change → same test passes`

and:

`test command fails → same command passes → no corresponding file edit`

These can indicate that an agent changed a test instead of fixing the underlying issue.

Rashomon currently runs as a Claude Code plugin or through the CLI.

CLI:

`rashomon watch`

then:

`rashomon report`

Plugin:

`/rashomon:report`

There are still edge cases around cwd, git state, test-selection arguments, generated files, retries, and parallel execution. I would be interested in feedback from people building agents on what execution signals you would want Rashomon to capture or correlate.

GitHub: https://github.com/altrace-dev-role/rashomon

title.value: Show HN: Rashomon – An independent execution record for AI coding agents

story_text.value:
Hi guys,

Posted this (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48832797) on HN a few months ago when it was a different product (and closed source). It was originally a way of managing multiple agents in parallel (like TMUX, but with a nicer chat UI).

But I found that I was only able to work with 3 or 4 agents simultaneously without information overload, so I decided to morph it into something which resembles Slack, where you can either privately speak to agents or address a room (like a channel) full of them. Importantly though, the agents can delegate work to each other, create other agents etc.

Also had lots of user feedback from the first launch which means we've added multiple harnesses (Codex, OpenCode and waiting for Anthropic to approve Claude Code), git worktrees, connections to hundreds of MCPs, CLIs and APIs, browser-use and a proactive Chief of Staff (which periodically wakes up and gets things moving). It's local with no telemetry.

Grateful for the feedback from our users from the first launch. Would be grateful for bug reports, other problems, ideas, questions or suggestions.

Thanks, Chris

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Hongyin. I built Vibivibi (https://vibivibi.com) because I kept starting a coding agent session on my laptop and wanting to continue it on a server, or hand it to a colleague. I want an easier way to do it but won’t trust anyone hosting my traces who promises they won’t sell it (market price per coding trace is $50 to $100).

What Vibivibi does: a small CLI, `vibi`, finds the sessions your coding agents keep locally (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Pi), encrypts one on your machine and uploads it. On another machine `vibi pull` puts it back where the agent expects it, so `claude --resume <id>` just continues. `vibi push` can also send a session to someone else by email.

Our service cannot read session content. Each user has a key pair made on their first machine; the private key reaches the server only wrapped with a key derived from an encryption password that never leaves the user's machines. Every session version is encrypted with its own random key, which is then wrapped for each recipient (X25519, HKDF, AES-256-GCM). The server sees account emails, public keys, machine names, sizes, timestamps, who sent what to whom, and an optional plain-text label.

Sending to someone who doesn't have an account yet works too: the sender's client makes a key pair on their behalf, locks it with a random 12-character passphrase, and shows the sender that passphrase to pass on out of band. When the recipient signs up and enrolls a machine, their client unlocks it locally and re-keys the session to their own key.

The client is open source (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/subconscious-systems/vibi-cli The crypto and the schemas of everything the client sends live in one package, so the claims above can be checked against the code. It ships as a single executable, no Node or npm needed: `curl -fsSL https://vibivibi.com/install.sh | sh`, or build it yourself. The server (Next.js on Vercel, Postgres, blob storage) is not open source.

Pricing: free for 200 MB of encrypted storage and unlimited sends; Pro is $8/month for 20 GB; Team is $15/seat with an admin view and a "send only inside the team" policy.

Honest limitations: - There is no password recovery. Forget the encryption password and the key, and everything encrypted for it, is gone.

I'd like to hear where the threat model falls short, and which agents or workflows you'd want supported next.

title.value: Show HN: Vibivibi – End-to-end encrypted sharing of Coding Agent sessions

story_text.value:
I kept having ideas away from my desk, and my Claude Code sessions only lived at it. The hosted sessions run on a cloud copy of the repo, so my local hooks and config don't come along.

This is a small Node agent on a Windows PC (zero dependencies, binds to 127.0.0.1 only) exposed through tailscale serve, plus a PWA. Tap a folder on the phone and it starts a Claude Code session there with --remote-control, which you then drive from the Claude app. It's a start button, not a terminal.

The trade is spelled out in the README: a session runs with your account's full permissions and anything on your tailnet can reach the agent, behind a six-digit passcode with a lockout. Fine for a single-user tailnet, not for a shared one.

Windows only for now. Happy to answer questions about the design.

title.value: Show HN: Claude Remote – start Claude Code on your own PC from your phone

story_text.value:
A personal agent harness lives in your existing browser, connects to your claude-code (or any other major harness codex or cursor-cli...) NOT the SDK API, exposes web-optimized tools to the harness - that's Browsentic.

A free, opensource (Apache 2.0) with rich capabilities alternative to Comet, BrowserOS, Browser-use, Claude for Chrome or nanobrowser.

The unique architecture of Browsentic makes it different from all other alternatives. It uses a loopback MCP server that spawns claude/codex/OpenCode/Cursor harness in a detached process. You can already guess, it is a bi-directional MCP, you can browse agentic through the browser harness or through any MCP client.

Browsentic doesn't require any new browser to install and not limited to chromium, it supports Firefox as well. By default you don't even need CDP to perform core agentic browsing.

Capabilities: core accessibilities (50+ compare to nanobrowser only had 20), custom skill, record-replay, schedule-monitoring-notification, resolves captcha autonomously, has it's own memory, voice orb over web-speech API, can sideload custom tools, platform + browser + agent agnostic

It is opensource, no API key, no telemetry & local first and actively maintained and yesterday was the first public stable launch (v0.8.0)

Currently I'm the only author but every & any contribution or suggestion will be more than welcome :)

Source: https://github.com/imshaikot/browsentic

Install guide: https://browsentic.com/install

Docs: https://browsentic.com/docs

Install video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o8t4l9Q9BkE

story_text.value: I got recently laid off and wanted to learn and play with tools that are popular today as an exercise. Homebrew has some interesting analytics, but it only provides snapshots, you don't have a feel how the popularity of competing tools and technologies changed over time. So I started to take weekly snapshots of the last 30 days data of both formulas and casks. While I had some initial success with clustering packages based on their descriptions, but so far I wouldn't leave it on autopilot. However it serves as a reasonable basis for manual curation. I'd appreciate ideas on how to improve identifying packages of the same domain. (https://github.com/greg76/toth) One of the first surprises for me was that how Codex has been gaining momentum for the last two months compared to Claude Code. Also, while I was looking into the data rolling in, the drop of downloads across the board looked suspicious. I have reached out to the homebrew team and they confirmed that 7.0.0 introduced a regression in analytics reporting and with a sameday fix 7.0.6 should be reporting data as before.
